expertInsight: PD2 is not a bigger PD1. PD1 asks what a feature does; PD2 gives you a situation and asks which design holds up when 200 records arrive at once. The questions I found hardest were the async ones, where two options both work and you have to pick the one that survives a retry or a chained job. Know the governor limits cold, and be able to read a trigger and say what breaks it in bulk. Check the official exam guide for the current requirements, since Salesforce has changed what sits alongside the exam over the years.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Platform Developer II Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: PD2 is one of the harder Salesforce exams. It assumes you can read Apex and reason about it, so there is little to memorise. Most questions describe code or a requirement and ask which approach is correct in bulk, under governor limits, and when something fails.
bullets: 60 multiple-choice questions in 120 minutes, which is longer than most non-architect exams.
70% to pass, about 42 correct answers. That is a higher bar than PD1.
Code reasoning. Expect to be shown logic and asked what happens with 200 records, or after a retry.
Check the guide for extras. Salesforce has at times paired this credential with hands-on requirements, so confirm the current ones in the official exam guide.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Most people who pass have a couple of years writing Apex daily. Before you book. Aim for 80% or more on practice tests, and make sure you can write a trigger handler and a batch class from memory.

examFormat.heading: Platform Developer II Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions give you a short piece of logic or a requirement and ask which approach is right. The most common pattern is code that works for one record and fails for 200, where you pick the fix.
bestWayToPass: Write everything in bulk: No queries or DML inside loops, collect records and act once. Half the wrong answers break this rule.
Know the async options apart: Future methods, Queueable, Batch and Scheduled Apex each have different limits and uses. Queueable is the one that chains and keeps state.
Learn the common patterns: One trigger per object with a handler class, and separating queries from business logic.
Test like the exam does: Create your own data, mock callouts, and use Test.startTest and Test.stopTest so async work actually runs.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests advanced Apex: designing code that works in bulk, choosing the right asynchronous approach, integrating with outside systems, writing real tests, and keeping data secure. The exam is 60 scored questions in 120 minutes, with a 70% pass mark, weighted towards Process Automation, Logic, and Integration (27%) and User Interface (20%).

keyConcepts.h2: Platform Developer II: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Designing Apex That Scales
blocks.body: Most PD2 questions come back to one idea: code must work for 200 records as well as one. Never put a SOQL query or a DML statement inside a loop. Query once into a map, work in memory, then update once at the end. Use **one trigger per object** that calls a **handler class**, so the order of operations is clear and the logic can be tested on its own. Keep queries selective on large objects, since a filter on an unindexed field will time out once the table is big. Know the key limits by heart: 100 SOQL queries, 150 DML statements, 50,000 records retrieved, and 10,000 records per DML in a synchronous transaction.

blocks.heading: Asynchronous Apex: Picking the Right One
blocks.body: **Future methods** are the simplest. They take only primitive parameters, cannot be chained, and give you no job ID to track. **Queueable** is the usual modern choice: it accepts objects, returns a job ID, can be chained to run one job after another, and can hold state. **Batch Apex** processes large volumes in chunks, each chunk with its own governor limits, which is how you touch millions of records. **Scheduled Apex** runs on a timetable and usually just starts a batch job. Async transactions get higher limits, for example 200 SOQL queries and a longer CPU allowance, which is often the reason to move work off the main transaction.

blocks.heading: Integration: Callouts, Named Credentials and Events
blocks.body: A trigger cannot make a callout directly. Move the work to a future method marked for callouts or, better, to a Queueable. Store endpoints and credentials in **Named Credentials** so no secret appears in code. Remember the limits: 100 callouts per transaction and 120 seconds total. For loose coupling, publish a **Platform Event** and let subscribers react, which means the publisher does not fail when a subscriber is down. **Change Data Capture** sends field-level changes automatically. In tests, callouts must be mocked with Test.setMock, because tests cannot reach the network.

blocks.heading: Testing: Data, Mocks and Coverage
blocks.body: Tests must build their own data. Use **@TestSetup** to create it once for all methods in the class, and avoid SeeAllData, which makes tests depend on whatever happens to be in the org. Wrap the code under test in **Test.startTest** and **Test.stopTest**, which resets limits and forces queued async work to run before you assert. Mock callouts with **HttpCalloutMock**, and use **Test.isRunningTest** sparingly. You need 75% coverage to deploy, but coverage is not the goal: assert the result, test the bulk case, and test the failure case.

blocks.heading: Security in Apex: Sharing, Field Access and Exposure
blocks.body: Apex runs in system mode by default, which ignores the user's record access. **With sharing** makes a class respect the user's sharing, **without sharing** ignores it, and **inherited sharing** takes whichever applies to the caller. Sharing does not cover fields: check field-level security with **Security.stripInaccessible** or **WITH USER_MODE** so a user cannot read or write a field they should not see. Use **WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED** in SOQL where it fits. Any method marked **@AuraEnabled** is reachable from the front end, so validate its input and check access inside it.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Platform Developer II Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions give you code or a requirement and several approaches that look reasonable. The right answer is nearly always the one that still works in bulk, respects limits, and fails safely.

blocks.heading: Bulk Safety First
blocks.body: If an option has a query or DML inside a loop, it is wrong. Collect into collections and act once.

blocks.heading: Choosing an Async Option
blocks.body: Objects as parameters, chaining or job tracking means Queueable. Millions of records means Batch. A timetable means Scheduled.

blocks.heading: Integration Decisions
blocks.body: Callouts leave triggers through async Apex. Named Credentials hold the endpoint and auth. Platform Events decouple publisher from subscriber.

blocks.heading: Trigger Design
blocks.body: One trigger per object, logic in a handler class, and no recursion. This is the pattern the exam expects.

blocks.heading: Test Design
blocks.body: Build your own data, mock callouts, wrap in start and stop test, and assert the outcome rather than chasing coverage.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications After Developer
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Platform Developer II:

sampleQuestions.question: Which design pattern is recommended for creating a single instance of a class that can be reused throughout the transaction?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Singleton Pattern ensures only one instance of a class is created and provides a global point of access to it.
whyWrong: Factory Pattern creates objects of varying types based on input, but doesn't guarantee a single reusable instance.
Decorator Pattern adds behavior to an object dynamically; it doesn't restrict instantiation to one instance.
Strategy Pattern swaps interchangeable algorithms at runtime, it's about behavior, not instance control.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the @TestSetup annotation?
options: To bypass governor limits in tests
To create test data once that can be used by all test methods in the class
sampleQuestions.explanation: @TestSetup creates test data once at the beginning of the test class, and that data is available to all test methods, improving test performance.
whyWrong: @TestSetup creates real records via DML, not mocks, mocking external callouts requires HttpCalloutMock instead.
@TestSetup has no effect on governor limits; each test method still runs under standard limits.
@TestSetup does not affect test parallelization, that's controlled separately via test class settings.

sampleQuestions.question: Which approach should be used to make callouts from a trigger?
options: Make the callout directly in the trigger
sampleQuestions.explanation: Callouts cannot be made directly from triggers. Use @future(callout=true) or Queueable with Database.AllowsCallouts to make asynchronous callouts.
whyWrong: Database.executeBatch starts a batch job asynchronously but doesn't itself make an HTTP callout, you'd still need callout logic inside the batch's execute method.
Triggers cannot make callouts directly: Salesforce throws a runtime error because triggers run inside an existing transaction that can't be safely suspended.
Platform Events solve pub/sub messaging, not the specific restriction on synchronous callouts from trigger context.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the benefit of using Platform Events over traditional triggers for integration?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform Events provide loosely coupled, asynchronous communication between systems, making integrations more scalable and maintainable.
whyWrong: Platform Events are asynchronous by nature, so they're not faster for real-time execution, the benefit is decoupling, not speed.
Platform Events don't inherently lower governor limits, they run under standard Apex limits like any other transaction.
Error handling isn't better by default with Platform Events; failed subscribers still need their own retry/error logic.

sampleQuestions.question: Which interface should be implemented to allow a batch job to be chained?
sampleQuestions.explanation: To chain batch jobs, you call Database.executeBatch in the finish method of the current batch job to start the next batch.
whyWrong: Database.Stateful only preserves instance variable values across batch execute calls; it has nothing to do with chaining to a new job.
Database.Batchable is the interface a batch class implements, but implementing it alone doesn't chain jobs.
Database.AllowsCallouts permits HTTP callouts inside a batch job; it doesn't enable chaining to another batch.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the Database.Stateful interface in batch Apex?
options: To retain instance variable values between batch executions
sampleQuestions.explanation: Database.Stateful preserves instance variable values across batch iterations.
whyWrong: Database.Stateful has no effect on execution speed, its purpose is state retention, not performance.
Database.Stateful does not bypass or raise governor limits, each batch chunk still runs under normal limits.
Database.AllowsCallouts is the separate interface needed to permit callouts in batch Apex.

sampleQuestions.question: Which design pattern helps decouple trigger logic from business logic?
options: Trigger Handler pattern with service classes
sampleQuestions.explanation: Trigger Handler pattern separates trigger logic from business logic for maintainability.
whyWrong: Factory alone handles object creation logic, not the separation of trigger and business logic layers.
Decorator alone adds behavior to objects dynamically, it's unrelated to organizing trigger-to-handler flow.
Singleton alone controls instance creation; it doesn't structurally separate trigger code from business logic.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the benefit of using Queueable Apex over @future?
options: Chaining jobs, passing complex types, and getting job IDs
sampleQuestions.explanation: Queueable supports chaining, complex parameters, and job ID tracking.
whyWrong: Queueable Apex has the same governor limits as @future in most respects, lower limits isn't the actual benefit.
Queueable isn't inherently faster than @future; both run asynchronously on the same execution model.
Queueable Apex runs asynchronously, just like @future; it does not run synchronously.

sampleQuestions.question: Which security consideration applies when exposing Apex to LWC?
options: Use @AuraEnabled with proper FLS and sharing checks
sampleQuestions.explanation: Apex exposed to LWC must enforce FLS and sharing rules.
whyWrong: Apex exposed to LWC always requires enforcing security; 'no security needed' is never correct for user-facing code.
Sharing alone is insufficient; field-level security must also be enforced so users can't see restricted fields.
FLS alone is insufficient; sharing rules must also be respected so users only see records they're permitted to access.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the Strategy pattern enable?
options: Interchangeable algorithms encapsulated in separate classes
sampleQuestions.explanation: Strategy pattern allows swapping algorithms at runtime.
whyWrong: Single instance control describes the Singleton pattern, not Strategy.
Event handling is a separate concern (often solved with Observer pattern), not what Strategy addresses.
Object creation is the concern of creational patterns like Factory, not Strategy.

sampleQuestions.question: Which governor limit applies to heap size in Apex?
options: 6 MB for synchronous, 12 MB for asynchronous
whyWrong: 1 MB is far below the actual synchronous heap limit of 6 MB.
6 MB applies only to synchronous Apex, asynchronous contexts get a higher limit, so this option is incomplete.
Apex heap size is never unlimited; Salesforce enforces strict limits to protect the multi-tenant platform.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Test.isRunningTest()?
options: To conditionally alter logic when code runs in test context
sampleQuestions.explanation: Test.isRunningTest() detects test context for mock responses or conditional logic.
whyWrong: Test.isRunningTest() doesn't skip tests; it lets code branch its behavior when running inside a test context.
It has no effect on execution speed; it's a conditional check, not a performance optimization.
It doesn't bypass governor limits; those still apply identically whether or not code is running in a test.

sampleQuestions.question: Which interface allows Apex to be invoked by Process Builder or Flow?
sampleQuestions.explanation: InvocableMethod exposes Apex to Flow and Process Builder.
whyWrong: @AuraEnabled exposes Apex methods to Lightning components (LWC/Aura), not to Flow or Process Builder.
@RestResource exposes Apex as a REST web service endpoint, unrelated to Flow invocation.
A plain trigger cannot be invoked directly by Process Builder or Flow; it only fires on DML against its object.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a common use case for Platform Events?
options: Decoupling integrations, logging, and cross-org messaging
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform Events enable loosely coupled, event-driven architectures.
whyWrong: Batch processing is handled by Batchable Apex, a different mechanism from event-driven Platform Events.
Scheduled jobs are handled by the Schedulable interface, not Platform Events.
Platform Events are inherently asynchronous, they don't apply to synchronous-only trigger scenarios.

sampleQuestions.question: Which approach improves Apex test performance?
options: Create data in every test method
sampleQuestions.explanation: @TestSetup creates data once for all test methods, improving performance.
whyWrong: Creating data in every test method duplicates DML work and slows down the whole test class, the opposite of the correct approach.
Minimal assertions might make a test file shorter, but it doesn't affect execution performance and reduces test quality.
SeeAllData=true is discouraged because it ties tests to org data and can cause unpredictable, slower, and fragile test runs.
